title: Creating Awareness About a Problem or Opportunity Others Don’t Yet See
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post addresses a common problem for visionary leaders: when they simply announce a problem or opportunity they have spotted, teams often respond with skepticism and resistance. The author recommends inviting people into sense-making instead of telling them what to think. The leader surfaces signals, facts or patterns and asks the team what they make of them, using sample questions about customer complaints, metrics and repeated resource requests. Once the team helps name the issue, it becomes theirs, and co-ownership replaces the need for persuasion. A three-part formula is offered: reveal the facts and signals, frame why they caught your attention, then engage in shared curiosity. The closing argument is that leaders who get ahead of their team create needless resistance, whereas people who own a problem act as players rather than spectators.
points: Announcing what you see invites doubt; asking what the team makes of the evidence lowers defensiveness.
The post supplies a repeatable three-step formula: reveal facts and signals, frame why they matter, then invite shared curiosity.
Co-ownership of a diagnosis is presented as stronger than persuasion for winning buy-in.
The sample questions model how to open a conversation from concrete data rather than from the leader's conclusion.
Leaders who race ahead of the team are said to breed resistance that is unnecessary and potentially poisonous.
quotes: People resist being told what to think. The best leaders invite them into the sense-making process instead.

By revealing the facts and signals and engaging in shared curiosity, the leader not only highlights something that might be important but invites the team to reason along with them. This engaged curiosity naturally lowers defensiveness and increases interest in the topic.
The moment the team helps to identify the problem or opportunity, it becomes theirs. If the goal is buy-in for what the leader is seeing, co-ownership trumps the need for persuasion every time.
Think about the formula for creating awareness and buy-in like this: Reveal the facts and signals, frame why it has caught your attention, and then engage in shared curiosity.
Remember that it’s not about convincing others about what you see. It’s about guiding them to discover it along with you.
Savvy leaders too often get ahead of the team and fail to bring them along for the ride. The resistance they foster in the process is both unnecessary and potentially poisonous.
People who own problems and opportunities are never spectators. They become players who charge forward with action and ideas.
